paras: The lynching of Robert Barker was the shooting of a Black prisoner by an armed group of Black men on the road from Okolona to Houston, in Chickasaw County, Mississippi, on July 30, 1881.
Barker, accused of killing Luther White, a Black man, about three weeks earlier, was taken from an officer about five or six miles from Okolona, carried into the woods and shot dead.
White papers headlined the case as a Black murderer "Lynched by a Mob of His Own Color," and the Okolona paper said the victim had received "a justly merited punishment."

According to the Chickasaw Messenger of Okolona, Luther White was killed on a Saturday night in early July 1881 outside a colored church on the plantation of John Jolly. The paper named the accused as "Sam Robinson alias Rob Barker" and said both men had been drawn to the same young woman, who favored White. In its account the assailant struck White with a heavy piece of wood at the church door and then stabbed him, and onlookers failed to stop him from escaping.

Other versions differed on the details: a Tennessee state brief said Robinson beat White's brains out with a pine knot, while the Okolona dispatch of July 30 placed the killing at White's house and described a club and a knife.

On Friday evening, July 29, Barker was brought into Okolona and handed to the authorities by a group the Messenger put at "at least one hundred armed men, mostly colored." He was jailed and guarded overnight, and on Saturday morning he waived examination before the mayor and was committed. Because the Okolona jail was not secure, Officer Buford was told to take him to the county jail at Houston, about twenty miles away.

The Messenger reported that a large and excited crowd gathered in town that morning, where some threatened to lynch him, and that the officers tried to slip the prisoner out without its knowledge. By its account a party of nearly one hundred waited on the road at Shaw creek bottom, about five miles out, while others followed the officer from town. There twenty or thirty colored men stepped into the road, seized the bridle of the mule Barker was riding, and hurried him into a thicket, where "the report of twenty guns" was heard.

Buford, the paper said, could only beg for the prisoner's life and protest the "unlawful act," and the crowd dispersed after the shooting, leaving the body on the ground. The dispatch said Barker "pleaded earnestly for his life, but without effect."
No report of an inquest, arrests or grand jury action appears in the coverage. State briefs in mid-August recorded it as a lynching by Black men.

The first report was an Okolona dispatch dated July 30 that ran in the Memphis Daily Appeal the next day under the headline "A Negro Murderer Lynched by a Mob of His Own Color." It treated Barker's guilt as settled and closed: "Justice was meted out to him properly by men of his own color." The Weekly Clarion of Jackson reprinted the same dispatch on August 11 without that final sentence.

The Chickasaw Messenger, the local weekly, called Barker a "desperado" and "the slayer of three men" and said that while it did not approve of mob law, he had received a "justly merited punishment." In a separate paragraph the same issue mocked the prospect of a jailhouse conversion, remarking that Barker "would have made a saint in glory" had the "wicked mob" given him time to repent.
Later Mississippi briefs garbled the victim's name as "Robert Walker" in the Panola Star and "Bob Booker" in the Brookhaven Ledger.

The papers disagreed on the date, with the Okolona reports placing the lynching on Saturday, July 30, and the Panola Star on the 29th. They also gave different sizes for the party that killed him: twenty or thirty men in the road and nearly one hundred waiting in the Messenger, about sixty in the Panola Star, and an unnumbered "armed mob" in the dispatch.

reader.title: Lynching of Robert Barker
bases: An armed group took Barker from an officer escorting him to jail and shot him dead in the woods (A3, A4).

Barker was shot dead by twenty or thirty men (about twenty guns) after they seized him from Officer Buford, who protested the 'unlawful act' (A4); the papers presented it as punishment for the murder of Luther White, 'Justice was meted out to him' (A3).

The Okolona dispatch (A3) and the Messenger's fuller local narrative (A4) agree on the seizure from the officer on the Houston road and the shooting in the woods, with different details; later briefs (A7, A9) agree on the core.

accounts.label: State briefs
accounts.gist: A colored man, named as Robert Walker or Bob Booker, who killed Luther White, was lynched near Okolona by about sixty armed men of his own color / a band of negroes.

framing.detail: Headline 'A Negro Murderer Lynched by a Mob of His Own Color'; closes 'Justice was meted out to him properly by men of his own color.'
Calls Barker a 'desperado' and 'slayer of three men'; disclaims mob law but calls the killing a 'justly merited punishment' and a warning.
Sarcastic paragraph mocking the idea that Barker might have been converted on the scaffold.
One-sentence state briefs recording the lynching without comment.
